description:
Mohra Sharif is a celebrated *khanqah* — a Sufi lodge and spiritual centre — set in a small village in the Murree hills of the Punjab, some distance above Islamabad and Rawalpindi. It is the home of the *Naqshbandi Mujaddidi Qasimiya* order, and takes its name (the "holy village") from its sanctity. The centre was established by *Khwaja Muhammad Qasim Sadiq*, born about 1846 (1263 AH), whose forebears are said to have migrated from Iran and settled in the Rawalpindi district. According to the traditions of the order, he journeyed on foot to the shrine of his spiritual guide, *Khwaja Nizamuddin Aulia* of Kahiyan Sharif in the Neelam Valley of Kashmir, and there received *khilafat* with the instruction to settle at Mohra Sharif. He is said to have undertaken a *chilla* — a forty-day retreat of unbroken devotion — and the stone slab on which he sat throughout is preserved at the shrine as a relic (*tabarruk*). On his death the spiritual seat passed to his son Khwaja Pir Muhammad Zahid Khan, remembered as the first *sajjada nashin* (custodian) of Mohra Sharif, and thence down a line of successors. The khanqah remains an active centre of Naqshbandi devotion, drawing pilgrims especially at its annual *urs*, and is counted among the important Sufi shrines of the northern Punjab.

The khanqah's own historical account names the specific line of succession only broadly gestured at above: Khwaja Pir Muhammad Zahid Khan, the founder's third son and first *sajjada nashin*, is recorded as having died on 9 December 1993; he was followed by Hazrat Khawaja Pir Badshah Sahib, who died on 13 August 2008; and then by Pir Auliya Badshah Farooq Sahib as the third *Sajjada Nasheen*. In January 2026, the German Ambassador to Pakistan, Ina Lepel, visited the khanqah — described in press coverage as a "200-year-old Sufi centre" — and met with its custodian, named in that report as Pir Mujtaba Farooq Gull; a second report of the same visit notes that she spent considerable time at the khanqah's attached madrassa, observing classes and discussing curriculum with students.

## Bibliography

- "German envoy visits historic shrine," *The Express Tribune*, 8 January 2026.
- "German Ambassador visits madrassa in Mohra Sharif," *Islamabad Post*, 13 January 2026.
- "Guide to Mohra Sharif," mohrasharif.com, accessed 16 August 2026.
qa_note: This addition rests substantially on a single, non-independent source: the khanqah's own website (mohrasharif.com), for the founder's name, order, and succession details already given in this Description's main text, corroborated only by two January 2026 press reports (The Express Tribune, Islamabad Post) that confirm the shrine's existence, its approximate age ("200-year-old"), and its current custodian, but say nothing about its founding history. This addition has not yet been corroborated by an independent scholarly source and should be read accordingly. Separately, a discrepancy exists across sources on the founder's death year: the khanqah's own site gives "20th November of 1943," while Wikipedia (not independently verifiable here) gives conflicting birth years (1822, 1845, 1846) and death years (1942, 1943) within the same article; this could not be resolved because none of the underlying sources on either side were independently fetchable in this research pass, and is reported here as an open gap rather than a resolved fact.
